articles.title: From Russia to India: Meet Yury Lisichko, the man fixing shooters' pistol grips
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: There are tools on the table, pieces of wood on the floor, and pistol grips in various stages of modification. Some tools hang around the room.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: There are tools on the table, pieces of wood on the floor, and pistol grips in various stages of modification. Some tools hang around the room. His T-shirt and eyelashes are covered with wooden husk. A few used coffee mugs are lying around.Two cats wander in and out.This is Yury Lisichko's workshop in Greater Noida, where Indian shooters arrive with a problem that can be difficult to explain and even harder to fix: the grip of their pistol does not feel right.Lisichko looks at the weapon, studies the shooter's hand and wrist, examines the existing grip and starts working on it. The shooter then takes the pistol into another room and aims at a target.A few shots are followed by more adjustments, and then more shot follow. The process continues until Lisichko is satisfied with the grip and the shooter is comfortable with it."I know the mentality of every shooter. I speak to them for one or two minutes... that's it. I get the problem. Now, I tell them to be seated until I am done. They wait, I work and when I am ready I give them targets to shoot. First, I need to be satisfied and then them. I make grips with a fresh piece of wood. I don't use old wood or just paste and give them. I want these shooters to do well," Lisichko told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview.Shooters have been coming to him for years. Anish Bhanwala, Jitu Rai, Manu Bhaker and Sarabjot Singh are among those he has worked with. juniors, seniors, and international shooters all come, even during major competitions, and the door remains open."Anish [Bhanwala] came to me just ahead of the Asian Games. He spent the entire day here. When the solution didn't come, he decided to stay here to avoid much travel. Many Commonwealth Games and Asian Games shooters came to me. Shooters come here, stay too. They order their food and play with my cats. All I tell them is, 'Don't disturb me,'" Lisichko said.However, Lisichko did not come to India to become a grip specialist. He arrived in 2009 as a foreign pistol shooting coach.The 200-page CV that brought him to IndiaIn 2007, Lisichko was involved with the European Championships in St Petersburg. After the competition, foreign coaches asked him why they had never seen him work abroad with athletes.He decided to put together a CV, that too a 200-page one containing his education, the athletes he had worked with in Russia, his achievements and other details of his career.Two years later, he got a call from India."That was the first time when I heard Indian English. It's absolutely not understandable. I remember that conversation. I could not understand the accent much. He disconnected the call saying, 'Call me later with someone who speaks good English, please," Lisichko recalled.The Indian Army wanted him to work in India. At the Indian embassy, he was shown an order from the Defence Ministry concerning the appointment of foreign coaches for the Army.He said yes. His visa was ready the next day and Lisichko landed in New Delhi, travelled to Indore and then reached Mhow - a cantonment town in Indore, Madhya Pradesh."I had no knowledge about India. I knew this was a country with a lot of wild animals and snakes everywhere, spiders everywhere. But with time, I realised it is beautiful. I have travelled around India and met different people. Everyone is different," he said.He started working with Army shooters, including at the Infantry School in Mhow and the Army Marksmanship Unit. He also worked with India's junior pistol shooting setup and later with senior athletes.For the first three or four months, the accent, more than the language was a problem. Slowly, he began speaking in a similar way. Then came Hindi, Indian food, and the small exchanges that came with everyday life in the country."Namaste. Namaskaar. Kaise ho. Theek ho. Kaha jaa rahe ho. When I go to the market, I have learnt to say, 'Kitna hua bhaiya? Mere paise wapas do.' I have learnt that Hindi is a very simple language. And it's so far from techniques. It seems like the Ukrainian language. Because I am ethnically Ukrainian. But you see, my heart is with Ukraine, my brain is partly in Russia," Lisichko said.How the coach became the man shooters call for gripsLisichko had studied technology at Moscow Aviation University and had experience working with wood and other materials. His work with pistol grips developed gradually.The first attempts did not go smoothly. "The first grip was destroyed, the second grip was destroyed. After that I made a grip with which I started to work. And began to improve my level in shooting. With time I excelled in the art of making grips," he recalled.That work eventually became a specialised part of what he does for shooters."I didn't know the study in woods, experience would become a specialised craft and I will be now helping shooters in fixing grips ahead of competitions. When they win, I silently pat on my back too (laugh)," Lisichko said.There is no standard grip that can simply be transferred from one shooter to another. The same pistol can feel different in different hands."You can buy the same rifle as Abhinav Bindra. You can buy the same pistol as Manu Bhaker or Jitu Rai or Vijay Kumar. You can buy a shooting suit the same as Bindra. Shooting boots like Bindra. You can use the same pellets, the same gloves, everything. But you can't shoot with the same grip. Every human hand and the ability to hold something are different. So grip is something that makes a shooter uncomfortable and destroys their focus," he said.That is why the pistol sometimes arrives at Lisichko's workshop before it reaches the competition range. The shooter has to wait as he works on the wood, and then comes another set of shots and recalibration.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Her mother thought she was in Bengaluru. Seema Kumari was actually winning Asian Games bronze in Nagoya
articles.summary: On Thursday night, when a beaming Seema Kumari took a short lap of honour draped in the tricolour, congratulatory messages began pouring in.
articles.body: On Thursday night, when a beaming Seema Kumari took a short lap of honour draped in the tricolour, congratulatory messages began pouring in. It was perhaps then that her mother realised her daughter was in Nagoya and not Bengaluru.Seema’s 75-year-old mother, who lives in Reta in Himachal Pradesh, suffers from hypertension. Concerned about her daughter’s well-being, she is often kept in the dark about Seema’s travels and competitions.But after the stupendous performance Seema delivered on a windy night at the Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium, her mother will have plenty to celebrate. So will a nation, after the 25-year-old opened India’s athletics medal account with a bronze in the women’s 10,000m.In a tight race, Seema clocked 32:50.05 to finish behind Bahrain’s Winfred Yavi (32:39.18) and Japan’s Nozomi Tanaka (32:41.54).Her bronze ended India’s 16-year wait for a medal in the event at the Asian Games. Preeja Sreedharan and Kavita Raut had won gold and silver respectively, at the 2010 Games.It was a race built on endurance, pace, persistence and planning. Up against a star-studded field, Seema could have been forgiven for feeling the pressure. Instead, she focused on the distance rather than the runners around her.Her consistency was remarkable. Across all 25 laps, she never fell out of the leading pack. With two laps to go, she even raised hopes of a silver, but Bahrain’s Yavi stepped on the gas at the 200m mark and Tanaka accelerated, leaving Seema to settle for bronze.For Seema, who lost her father at a young age and is one of six siblings, it was a special medal on her Asian Games debut.“The race was very tactical. Everyone ran for the medal and I also thought that I would fight for it. Although I’m happy that I’ve earned a medal in my first Asian Games, I hope to change the colour of the medal in the 5000 metres event.”The past year-and-a-half has seen Seema on a rising curve training under coach Scott Simmons.“I’ve been training with Simmons for the past three years and have been sent to the USA for camps and training. It is very beneficial because conditions are tough there and we train with Olympic champions,” she said. Seema won a silver at the World University Games last year.As expected, India’s medal of the day came from the 4x400m mixed relay team. In a thrilling comeback, the quartet of Manu Saji, MR Poovamma, Vishal TK and Vithya Ramraj clocked 3:14.46 to take silver behind Bahrain, who won gold in a Games-record timing of 3:12.87.India did not have the best of starts, with Manu unable to provide the initial momentum. Poovamma, however, hauled the team back into contention with a strong second leg.Vishal then closed the gap and put India firmly in medal bracket before Vithya produced an impressive anchor leg. With the Vietnam runner breathing down her neck, she held her nerve in the home straight to fend off the challenge. The Vietnamese quartet finished just 0.08 seconds behind with 3:14.54. Jay Kumar and Kiran Phal, who ran the morning heats, were replaced with Vishal and Vithya for the final.Asha Ilango narrowly missed out on a triple jump medal, finishing fourth behind China’s Li Yi on countback after both athletes recorded a best jump of 13.83m. Asha needed to better 13.79m with her final attempt to move ahead of Li, but could manage only 13.59m. The other Indian in the fray, Niharika Vashisht, finished 10th.Gurindervir Singh eased into the 100m semifinals. He clocked 10.38 seconds to finish second in Heat 4. articles.title: Lewis Hamilton put £20 million behind a promise to change Formula 1; here’s the foundation he built for motorsport’s future
articles.summary: Lewis Hamilton launched Mission 44 in July 2021 with a personal pledge of £20 million, using his success in Formula 1 to create more opportunities for
articles.body: Lewis Hamilton launched Mission 44 in July 2021 with a personal pledge of £20 million, using his success in Formula 1 to create more opportunities for young people from underrepresented backgrounds. The foundation grew from a problem Hamilton had seen throughout his racing career, the lack of Black people across motorsport, particularly in technical and engineering roles. Before launching Mission 44, he worked with the Royal Academy of Engineering on a 10-month study into those barriers. The Hamilton Commission later produced 10 recommendations, giving Hamilton a research-based plan for turning concern about representation into action.Why did Lewis Hamilton launch Mission 44 after looking at an F1 team photoThe idea did not start with a new charity. It started with Hamilton looking at an end-of-season Formula 1 photograph in 2019 and noticing how few Black faces were in it. The problem was bigger than the 20 drivers who compete in F1. Hamilton was looking at the thousands of people who design cars, build parts, work in factories, handle data and support teams away from the cameras.The Hamilton Commission was created with the Royal Academy of Engineering to understand why Black people were so underrepresented in British motorsport. Its report, “Accelerating Change: Improving Representation of Black People in UK Motorsport”, was published in July 2021 after 10 months of research. It looked at education, university admissions, apprenticeships, recruitment and workplace culture rather than treating the issue as something that started when a person applied for an F1 job.The report found that the UK motorsport sector employed about 40,000 people, while estimates from interviews suggested that less than 1% of people working in Formula 1 came from Black backgrounds. It also found that F1 teams often recruited engineering graduates from Russell Group universities, creating another barrier because Black engineering students were not spread evenly across those institutions.One figure showed just how early the problem could begin. In 2019, only two Black Caribbean students in the whole of England achieved an A* in A-level physics. The report also found that just over 3,800 Black students were studying engineering across UK universities, with about 820 at Russell Group universities.How did Lewis Hamilton turn that research into opportunities for Black studentsHamilton did not limit the response to racing teams. Mission 44 looked at the education pipeline first, because a person cannot enter an engineering job in motorsport if they have already been pushed away from science and maths years earlier.One early partnership was with Teach First. In October 2021, Mission 44 announced a two-year programme aimed at recruiting and training 150 Black STEM teachers for schools serving disadvantaged communities in England. The programme also included mentoring, research, networking and other efforts to understand how more Black graduates could be encouraged into STEM teaching.That approach connected directly to one of the Hamilton Commission’s findings. The report said Black Caribbean pupils were less likely to be placed in higher science sets and highlighted concerns around teacher expectations, school behaviour policies and access to science subjects. It also found that fewer than 10 Black students were studying motorsport qualifications in further education in 2019/20.Mission 44 also moved closer to motorsport itself. Through the Ignite partnership with Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS F1 Team, more than £5 million in seed funding was made available for projects designed to improve diversity and inclusion in motorsport. The partnership supported programmes ranging from grassroots participation to specialist engineering education.What has Lewis Hamilton’s Ignite partnership done for motorsport engineeringOne of the clearest examples is the motorsport engineering scholarship programme run with the Royal Academy of Engineering. The scheme was created after the Hamilton Commission identified the gap between Black students studying engineering and their chances of moving into motorsport.The first scholarship cohort was announced in 2023, with five students from Black or mixed Black backgrounds receiving financial and career support for motorsport-related master’s degrees. The programme has since expanded. In the 2024/25 period, eight new students received scholarships, with each getting a £28,000 grant alongside career development support.The programme is still developing. In January 2026, Mission 44 and the Royal Academy of Engineering announced an expanded version of the MSc Motorsport Scholarship. The new scheme offers scholarships worth up to £43,000 and is open to a wider group of candidates.Ignite also backed programmes outside engineering. Its first grants included support for Motorsport UK’s work to increase female participation in grassroots motorsport, showing that the partnership was not built around one route into the sport.How far has Lewis Hamilton’s Mission 44 grown since the £20 million pledgeMission 44 has since moved beyond its original focus on British motorsport. Its latest annual report says the foundation reached 550,000 young people during 2024/25 and expanded its work in the United States. It also launched an education policy campaign and continued funding organisations working on education and STEM access.That change is crucial because Hamilton’s original concern was never only about finding another Black Formula 1 driver. The Hamilton Commission showed that the barriers could appear much earlier, from school subject choices to access to technical education, university pathways and professional networks.The numbers also explain why Hamilton chose to build a foundation rather than simply make a one-time donation. The problem was spread across several stages of a young person’s life. Mission 44’s work has therefore included teachers, schools, engineering students, grassroots programmes and routes into employment.Five years after the £20 million pledge, the most visible part of Hamilton’s work is no longer just the amount of money attached to it. There is now a continuing structure behind the idea, research to identify barriers, partnerships to address them and scholarships and programmes designed to help young people move through the pipeline.The original photograph gave Hamilton a question. The Hamilton Commission helped define the problem, and Mission 44 became the vehicle for acting on it. In 2026, that work is still expanding, with the motorsport scholarship programme itself moving into a larger phase.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Brooke Hogan reveals relationship with father Hulk Hogan began to deteriorate "after he slept with" her friend
articles.summary: Hulk Hogan was not only credited as one of the greatest icons of professional wrestling, but also as a highly controversial person in real life.
articles.body: Hulk Hogan was not only credited as one of the greatest icons of professional wrestling, but also as a highly controversial person in real life. One of the biggest revelations came out in 2008 when his daughter's friend, Christiane Plante, admitted to the National Enquirer that they were romantically involved. Hogan's daughter Brooke reflected back on that situation and how it became a turning point in the relationship between her and her father.Brooke Hogan says her relationship with Hulk Hogan took a major turning point after an affair with her friendIn a recent interview with US Weekly, Brooke Hogan said, “A major turning point came after he slept with my friend Christiane [Plante]. I forgive people very easily — sometimes probably too easily — and I forgave him, but something between us changed afterward. I don’t think he ever related to me in quite the same way again.”This came on the heels of Hulk Hogan's divorce from his first wife, Linda. Both had filed for divorce in 2007 after being married for 24 years. Christiane Plante had revealed that their affair began after Hogan and Linda had come to the private realization that their marriage was over. After the affair revelation and divorce of her parents, Brooke said that the entire family structure changed.“Then the divorce happened, and our entire family structure changed. Over time, things became increasingly complicated until eventually the relationship I had always believed could survive anything couldn’t survive what was happening around us anymore”,she said.Brooke Hogan says she still loved her father Despite the years of pain and living in a family full of issues, betrayal, and controversies, Brooke did not want to erase the good memories of her father. However, she maintained that Hogan did hurt her at the same time.“I can love my father profoundly and still tell the truth about where he hurt me. I can acknowledge the wonderful things my family gave me while also acknowledging that eventually the dynamic became something I could no longer live inside. Both things can be true,” said Brooke.Hulk Hogan passed away due to a cardiac arrest in his home in Clearwater, Florida, in 2025. Brooke posted a heartfelt message after his passing and fondly remembered her father, much like the rest of the world, who loved Hogan despite his controversial reputation for much of his life.Also read: 'I got arrested'- WWE star Chelsea Green makes huge confession about her early yearsStay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Final mein gai, to gold hi layegi': Suruchi Inder Singh's coach after Asian Games 2026 triumph
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: “Final mein gayi, to gold hi layegi,” an elated Suresh Singh said after his student Suruchi Inder Singh helped India win its first gold medal
articles.body: NEW DELHI: “Final mein gayi, to gold hi layegi,” an elated Suresh Singh said after his student Suruchi Inder Singh helped India win its first gold medal of the day at the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, on Friday.Suruchi and her teammate Kamaljeet won gold in the 10m air pistol mixed team event, finishing on top at the Aichi General Shooting Range to give India its second gold medal of the Games.For Suruchi, the victory came after a disappointing individual event.The Haryana shooter, who won four individual World Cup gold medals in 2025 in Buenos Aires, Munich, Lima and Doha, including the World Cup Final, failed to qualify for the final in the individual 10m air pistol event. In a field of 55 shooters, she finished 26th in qualification with a score of 568-12x.“She was disappointed. But I knew she would come back stronger. She knows how to bounce back quickly, and that is her best quality. The moment she reached the final, I was 200 percent sure that she would win gold. That’s how she is,” the coach said.Suruchi's gold-winning showSuruchi and Kamaljeet were in control from the start of the mixed team final. The pair scored 103.0 in the first series of Stage 1, followed by 202.4 and 303.5. They continued their strong performance in Stage 2, scoring 364.7 in the first series and staying comfortably ahead of South Korea and Iran.After 18 shots, India remained at the top and extended their lead with a score of 424.9 in the second series of Stage 2.Suruchi and Kamaljeet eventually finished with a total score of 484.6 to win the gold medal.South Korea's Suhyeon Hong and Gaeun Choo finished second with 478.0. The Korean pair were 6.6 points behind the Indians, underlining India's control of the final.“She is an athlete for the finals. Look at her past record. If she has reached the final, then you can't stop her. She will go for gold. She doesn't want silver or bronze. She has that kind of hunger,” Suresh said.Hours of work before the Asian GamesAhead of the Asian Games, Suruchi worked on several aspects of her shooting with Suresh at his Guru Dronacharya Shooting Academy in Bhiwani.The coach said they focused on her technique, holding and dry-fire training. Suruchi's father had initially wanted her to take up wrestling.“She worked on her holding and did dry-fire training for hours to improve her focus. We also worked on some technical aspects,” he said.One of the key areas they focused on was timing.“The most important focus was on timing. I am a coach who focuses on timing and wants my shooter to finish the match early. I told the same thing to Suruchi. We used to decide a particular time and try to finish the shot within that time.“For example, if you have 60 seconds for one shot, finish that shot early. It helps you take the pressure off yourself and allows you to focus,” he said.Now, Suresh is waiting to welcome his student home.“I am just waiting for her. She has made everyone proud. We are eagerly waiting to welcome her,” the coach said.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Asian Games 2026: India one step away from defending kabaddi gold medals as men and women storm into finals
articles.summary: India’s kabaddi team continued their dominance at the Asian Games 2026 as both the men’s and women’s teams secured their places in the gold-medal matches
articles.body: India’s kabaddi team continued their dominance at the Asian Games 2026 as both the men’s and women’s teams secured their places in the gold-medal matches with semifinal victories. The women’s side defeated Nepal 48-24, while the men’s team followed with an emphatic 66-27 win over Thailand. The results ensured that India will have a chance to defend both kabaddi titles at the Aichi-Nagoya Games.For the women, the victory kept alive their bid for a fourth consecutive Asian Games gold medal. India have won the women’s kabaddi title at every Asian Games since the sport was introduced to the women’s programme in 2010.India women overpower NepalThe Indian women established control early and went into the interval with a 31-17 advantage. India combined successful raids with a disciplined defensive effort and repeatedly put Nepal under pressure. The four all-outs in the opening half gave the defending champions a substantial cushion.Nepal struggled to match India's intensity after the break. They managed only seven points in the second half as India maintained their advantage and eventually completed a 24-point victory.The win extended India's unbeaten run in the competition. They had previously defeated Iran, Bangladesh and Japan during the group stage. The defending champions will now turn their attention to the final, where they will look to maintain their remarkable record in the women's event.Men produce another dominant performanceThe men's team delivered an equally commanding performance against Thailand. India raced into an early lead and were comfortably ahead at 37-18 at half-time. Thailand showed flashes of resistance, with Theeradat Chaisit producing a strong spell in attack, but India quickly regained control.The Indian side continued to pile on the points after the break and eventually crossed the 50-point mark. Thailand could not keep pace with India's raiders and defenders as the gap continued to widen. India eventually closed out the semifinal with a 66-27 victory.India eye kabaddi doubleThe two semifinal victories mean India are now guaranteed medals in both kabaddi competitions. The women's team are chasing a fourth successive gold, while the men are aiming to retain the title they won at the previous Asian Games.India have historically dominated men's kabaddi at the Asian Games, having won eight gold medals since the sport made its debut in 1990. Iran are the only other nation to have won the men's title, doing so in 2018 when India had to settle for bronze.The Indian teams will now have one final hurdle to clear in Nagoya.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.body: NEW DELHI: Indian boxer Sachin Siwach moved to the men’s 60kg quarterfinals at the Asian Games 2026 in Aichi-Nagoya on Friday, beating Jordan’s Mohammad Adnan Abu Jajeh in a hard-fought contest to move within one win of securing a medal.The Commonwealth Games gold medallist, who received a first-round bye, had to dig deep to overcome his Jordanian opponent in a bout that turned into a tactical battle after an aggressive start. However, the contest soon settled into a tactical affair, with both boxers looking to counter their opponent’s attacks.The Indian’s cleaner punching earned him the opening round on three of the five judges’ scorecards. The second round followed a similar pattern, with the boxers cancelling each other’s attacks and waiting for openings.Needing to make up ground, Abu Jajeh pressed forward, allowing Sachin to find opportunities for sharp left-right combinations. Sachin stood his ground and traded blows, but appeared to tire in the closing stages, allowing his opponent to land a few clean punches.Despite the late pressure, the Indian had done enough to secure the split-decision win and progress to the last eight.Preeti Pawar to begin campaign later in the dayLater on Friday, India’s previous edition bronze medallist Preeti Pawar will begin her campaign in the women’s 54kg category.India had a mixed day in boxing on Thursday, with Parveen the only Indian to progress after receiving a walkover into the women’s 65kg quarterfinals. articles.title: Alex Lyon Injury Update Comes With Bad Sabres Forward News
articles.summary: The Buffalo Sabres were involved in plenty of goalie rumors in the offseason, but with their regular season opener next Thursday, nothing of that sort has co...
articles.body:
The Buffalo Sabres were involved in plenty of goalie rumors in the offseason, but with their regular season opener next Thursday, nothing of that sort has come to fruition.

For better or worse, it seems they plan to head into the new season with the same trio they had last year: Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen , Alex Lyon and Colten Ellis .

There's just one problem with that at the moment: Lyon is injured.

He started in the preseason on Thursday night, but he didn't finish.

Ellis had to come into the game to finish things off against the Detroit Red Wings in what turned out to be an overtime loss for Buffalo.

The result doesn't count yet, but the injury does. The Sabres will have no choice but to wait for more information.

Lyon left the Sabres' preseason game with the Red Wings on Thursday night midway through to be replaced by Colten Ellis.

As he left, Lyon was favoring his shoulder, according to The Athletic's Matthew Fairburn.

Fairburn didn't provide any later updates on social media other than that "the Sabres will return home with … new injuries to monitor."

Yep, it's not just Lyon — but hold that thought.

A Lyon injury would be particularly disappointing because of how well he played in the playoffs in his first season in Buffalo.

Lyon had a 90.6 save percentage in the regular season with a 2.77 goals against average. Then as part of the Sabres' first playoff appearance in 15 years, Lyon had a 90.4 save percentage and a 2.59 goals against average.

UPL and Ellis are quality goalies, too, but having Lyon in the fold again seemed like a massive plus.

Nothing is clear yet, but there's a chance the Sabres have to navigate without Lyon in the early going.

Kulich vanished a bit mysteriously from Thursday night's game.

After a shift in the middle of the second period, Kulich didn't return to the game. It wasn't clear what he may have hurt.

The Sabres at least open the season a couple days later than some teams. They play in Columbus against the Blue Jackets on Oct. 1, then have their home opener against Chicago on Oct. 3.

They'll give some hints as to how everyone is doing when they take on the Penguins in their final preseason game on Saturday.

Until then, Sabres fans will hold their breaths.

articles.title: It's official, Liverpool have signed another 'best' in the world
articles.summary: Liverpool believe they have signed another best in the world, the club just keeps getting better. There’s a real sense of excitement around Anfield right now...
articles.body:
Liverpool believe they have signed another best in the world, the club just keeps getting better.

There's a real sense of excitement around Anfield right now. Arne Slot and Richard Hughes have moved on, with Andoni Iraola and Julian Ward now back at the helm. In many ways, it feels like Liverpool are returning to what made them successful in the first place.

Iraola brings that charismatic, full-throttle style of football that Jurgen Klopp helped make synonymous with the Reds. Ward, meanwhile, has always had a squad-building mindset rather than simply chasing the biggest names available.

His previous track record speaks for itself. Ward was behind the decision not to sign Jude Bellingham , instead believing Liverpool needed a complete midfield rebuild. That decision ultimately paved the way for Ryan Gravenberch , Dominik Szoboszlai and Alexis Mac Allister arriving together the following summer.

Liverpool's plans to rebuild the squad is incredible

Ward's plans will be to build on the existing foundations that the Reds have already established. In his previous role at the club, he played a pivotal part of bringing in an exciting group of young players.

The basis of that team will be built on Florian Wirtz , Jeremy Jacquet , Dominik Szoboszlai and Bradley Barcola with Hugo Ekitike and Alexander Isak at the helm.

Iraola's fast-paced and intense style is going to get the best out of all of them. Patience is needed, but also behind the scenes Liverpool have more exciting players ready to step-up.

Trey Nyoni could be part of that conversation. Meanwhile, Lamine Camara has been pursued and a move for him is very possible come the January window.

Liverpool have signed another best in the world

The Reds have completed a lot of exciting new arrivals behind the scenes as well. They have recently started to aggresively pursue the market for young players.

In their attempts, Ward has played a key role alongside Matt Newberry and Pedro Marques to attract the best young players in the world to the club.

The Reds believe they've signed the best young goalkeeper on the planet with the arrival of Lucca Brughmans. But according to the Daily Mail, they also believe they've signed the best young defender on the planet as well.

The report claims that as well as Brughmans in Ifeanyi Ndukwe Liverpool believe they've signed the best young centre-back in the world.

So, in the future they could have two world-class players if they both fulfil their potential. It's exciting times ahead.

articles.title: Chiefs Share Kenneth Walker III News Amid Running Back’s Hot Start
articles.summary: The Kansas City Chiefs shared news that running back Kenneth Walker is leading the league in four key offensive categories. The post Chiefs Share Kenneth Wal...
articles.body:
Kansas City Chiefs running back Kenneth Walker III has unleashed a new aspect of the team's offense, reinvigorating the once-dormant rushing game.

The team shared some news on Walker's hot start, noting that he stands alone atop the leaderboard for several key offensive categories. The team's offseason acquisition of the reigning Super Bowl MVP has been one of the biggest contributors to their hot start, jumping out to 2-0 in a reverse of last year's early season struggles.

Kenneth Walker Leads NFL Amid Monster Start

As the team shared in a post on X, Walker has been one of the NFL's most productive running backs through the first two weeks of the season.

"Heading into Week 3, [Kenneth Walker] leads the league in rushing yards, scrimmage yards, broken tackles, and yards after contact," the team noted.

Walker has become the bell cow back for the Chiefs, a role that he was unable to play with the Seattle Seahawks and one the Chiefs avoided as they employed a running back by committee in recent years. He has taken to the role well, racking up 47 carries through two weeks and rushing for 290 yards with one touchdown.

Chiefs Face Warning on Kenneth Walker III Workload

Though Walker has been able to sustain his big workload through the first two games, ESPN's Nate Taylor suggested that the team will soon need to cut back on his carries to sustain him for the season.

"It's understandable why coach Andy Reid and offensive coordinator Eric Bieniemy wanted to put the ball in Walker's hands early and often," Taylor wrote. "Of course, Patrick Mahomes was returning from torn ligaments in his left knee, and undrafted rookie Kahlil Benson started at left tackle with Josh Simmons out because of a lower back injury. Walker, though, shouldn't continue to have 26 to 30 touches every game. The Chiefs also should give more opportunities to rookie Emmett Johnson, who has been productive in his limited carries."

The Chiefs have also hinted that they want to get more carries for Johnson in the coming weeks.

Even if the team does pull back on Walker's workload, his early season contributions have been critical as they allowed quarterback Patrick Mahomes to come back slowly from a torn ACL that cut short his 2025 season. Mahomes shook off a slow start in Week 1 and has shined since then, throwing for 566 total yards with five touchdowns through two weeks.

Indiana Pacers general manager Chad Buchanan has explained why the franchise brought back veteran forward James Johnson despite not having the cap space to keep him on the opening-night roster.

Johnson has agreed to an Exhibit 9 training camp deal and will join the Pacers for camp, with the franchise leaving the door open to potentially bring him back later in the season.

The 39-year-old spent parts of three seasons with Indiana between 2022 and 2025 before sitting out the 2025-26 season. Buchanan believes his value extends well beyond what he can provide on the court.

Chad Buchanan explains James Johnson's value to the Pacers

Buchanan made it clear that Johnson remains highly valued inside the organisation, particularly because of his experience and understanding of the Pacers' culture.

"No, I mean, obviously, you guys all know what what James means to our locker room, our culture. Um, you know, he's a guy that we've we have a real fondness for, obviously."

The Pacers cannot keep Johnson to begin the season because of their current salary-cap situation, but Buchanan sees training camp as an important opportunity for the veteran to contribute.

"There's value in him in our training camp situation because the training camp is a really big chance to set the table for your year. And both as how you play as a player, but also what you're about, you know, your system, your culture."

Buchanan also pointed to head coach Rick Carlisle's approach to training camp and Johnson's ability to help younger players understand what the coaching staff expects.

"Coach Carlo is a big believer in evaluating how guys play in training camp and having a veteran like James who understands what the coaches want. He understands the team, he understands the system… to help with, you know, establish what we're going to be about for the year was is going to be very valuable for us and he's he's just a guy you love having around."

There is no guarantee Johnson will return during the season, with Buchanan saying the Pacers will assess their health, performance and roster needs before making that decision.

Johnson's Exhibit 9 deal allows him to participate in camp without counting against the cap, while Indiana could have more flexibility later in the season. For now, the Pacers clearly see his presence as valuable as they prepare for a new campaign.

articles.title: 'Bosh', backlash and rebuild - how far can Fisher go?
articles.summary: British heavyweight Johnny Fisher - who returns to the Copper Box for his Zuffa Boxing debut on Saturday - reflects on defeat, fame and his rebuild.
articles.body:
When Johnny Fisher steps back inside the Copper Box Arena on Saturday night, the surroundings will feel familiar, even if much around his career has changed.

The east London venue was once something of a fortress for Fisher, where John Denver's 'Take Me Home, Country Roads' accompanied his ring walk and thousands of supporters reacted to every punch as his unbeaten record grew.

That changed last year when Dave Allen stopped him in the fifth round, handing the heavyweight his first professional defeat and leading critics to question his standing in the division.

Now the 27-year-old returns to headline against Belgium's Michael Pirotton in a 10-round contest which also marks his promotional debut for Dana White's Zuffa Boxing.

"Yeah, I had a loss, but one loss can't define your career," Fisher tells BBC Sport.

"There are many, many people before me who are much better than me who have lost and come back."

Fisher's rise has been far from conventional. With only a handful of amateur bouts and a background playing university rugby, he became a major domestic ticket-seller while still learning his trade.

Much of that appeal came alongside his father, 'Big John'. Their Chinese takeaway reviews, Essex humour and cries of "Bosh" found an audience beyond boxing and helped create the travelling support known as the Bosh Army.

Fisher won his first 13 professional fights, but his first meeting with Allen in December 2024 exposed vulnerabilities as he escaped with a controversial split-decision victory. Five months later, Allen stopped him in the fifth round, while his comeback against Ivan Balaz was also unconvincing despite a fourth-round stoppage win.

Those performances sharpened questions over Fisher's boxing credentials and exposed him to a harsher side of the attention that had accompanied his rise.

"Of course my fanbase is loyal to me," he says. "But when things are going well, people want to jump on the bandwagon and when it goes wrong there'll be people who are the first ones to say, 'we knew he'd never do it,' or 'he's no good.'"

There were also online jibes that Fisher was better suited to crossover boxing than the serious heavyweight scene, but he firmly rejects the suggestion his popularity makes him an influencer boxer.

"There are guys who have hardly any boxing experience whatsoever who have millions of followers on YouTube. You think of the Jake Pauls and the Tommy Furys, who aren't even at my level," he says.

"If people want to watch you and you've got a following - which I have through me and my dad - it's a magical thing. But it's not as if I'm in that influencer sphere. I'm a professional boxer first and foremost."

After five years with Eddie Hearn's Matchroom, Fisher signed with Zuffa Boxing in July, admitting the deal was simply too good to ignore.

"I got made a fantastic financial offer, which I would be lying if I said I could turn down," he says. "Our health isn't guaranteed in this sport, let alone our financials."

His first proper meeting with White came, suitably, over a Chinese meal with his father. "It was great to break bread - or prawn crackers - over a Chinese," Fisher adds.

There has been change in the gym too. Fisher left long-time trainer Mark Tibbs for Tony Sims and admits there had previously been an element of "winging it" in his preparation.

This camp, he says, has included around 160 rounds of sparring, altitude work and 6am hill sprints.

For all the change, though, Fisher's own assessment of his level remains relatively modest. "I'm not Usyk, I'm no AJ, I'm not Fury," he says. "I'm not these top guys at the top of the division."

He mentions Frazer Clarke and Solomon Dacres as possible domestic opponents and says fighting for the British title within 12 to 18 months would be "amazing".

Current champion Richard Riakporhe has already welcomed the prospect of facing him if Fisher beats Pirotton, although the former cruiserweight world-title challenger would represent a considerable step up.

"All I've got to do is win my next fight," Fisher adds. "That's the only thing that matters, and then the picture becomes clearer. My aspiration is always to have a good time and have a good old swing at it."

articles.title: Croft twins eye Joshua-Fury card in Cardiff
articles.summary: Welsh boxing twins Garan and Ioan Croft want a place on the Anthony Joshua v Tyson Fury undercard in Cardiff on Friday, 11 December.
articles.body:
Welsh boxing twins Garan and Ioan Croft are targeting a place on the Anthony Joshua v Tyson Fury undercard in Cardiff.

The long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight will take place at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.

The Croft brothers are also signed to Eddie Hearn's Matchroom company and Garan made no secret of his ambition following his latest win on Saturday.

"The one we both want is the Anthony Johsua v Tyson Fury undercard in Cardiff.

"It would be great to get some Welsh fighters out there on the undercard, including me and Ioan.

"It would be a dream come true to fight there. Our management will do everything we can to get us on that show and we want to go for it."

The twins rose to prominence at the 2022 Commonwealth Games in Birmingham, where Garan took bronze at light-middleweight level while Ioan won gold at welterweight.

Garan maintained his unbeaten run with a 90-second demolition of Italian fighter Mohammed Graich in Manchester.

The twins now both have 7-0 records since turning professional.

"I didn't learn much [from beating Graich] but I've had my learning fights now and it's about making statements," said Croft.

"I'm ready for bigger tests and hopefully a bigger occasion in December."

articles.title: Connecticut Sun wins its final game in front of sold-out crowd on emotional night
articles.summary: The Sun wrapped up their 24-year tenure in Connecticut with a 95-81 win as fans grieve the end of the franchise.
articles.body:
The Connecticut Sun and its fans lit up Mohegan Sun Arena one last time on Thursday night.

A packed house was on hand to see the Sun for the final time after 24 years in Connecticut as the team prepares to move to Houston for the 2027 season and beyond.

The Sun gave their home fans one last victory, topping the Toronto Tempo , 95-81, in front of a sold-out crowd.

After the final buzzer sounded, the seats at Mohegan Sun Arena were still full. Team president Jennifer Rizzotti let everyone in attendance know that the team would be signing autographs for whoever wanted to stay. Tables were set up across the court as fans poured down the aisles hoping to see their favorite players in person once more.

Aaliyah Edwards hugs Leila Lacan after the Sun's final game in Connecticut, a 95-81 win over the Toronto Tempo, on September 24, 2026 at Mohegan Sun Arena in Uncasville, Conn.Katie Morrison-O'Day

It was an emotional night filled with goodbyes, not just to the team, but to the community of fans that has been so passionate and loyal for the last 23 seasons.

Ariana Wilkinson is one of those fans for whom the Sun is more than just a basketball team. Wilkinson, wearing a Sun jersey she crocheted herself, was surrounded by people she had met through the fanbase.

"I've been coming to games for two seasons now," Wilkinson said. "It's meant so much. Everyone here has become family, and it's just been a great experience to get to know people and connect with everyone. It's just a family here."

Wilkinson shared an emotional moment with Sun guard Saniya Rivers , one of the most involved players when it comes to connecting with fans. Rivers was wearing her own personalized jersey, also crocheted by Wilkinson.

Sun guard Saniya Rivers hugs fan Ariana Wilkinson before the Connecticut Sun's final game at Mohegan Sun Arena in Uncasville, Conn. on September 24, 2026.Katie Morrison-O'Day

Rivers also made a big impact on Elsie Moreau, a youth basketball player who has been coming to games for the past couple of seasons.

"The players are the reason I keep going. I play basketball for them, basically," Moreau said. She talked about the relationships she's developed with players like Rivers and Edwards throughout the last couple of years.

The many Sun season-ticket holders in the crowd were recognized before the game with a show of thanks. Some, including Lois, who was in the crowd celebrating her 98th birthday on Thursday night, have owned season tickets since the Sun came to Connecticut from Orlando in 2003.

Debbie Elias has been attending Sun games for the past nine years. She made her way through the concourse before the game, hugging arena employees, some whose first names she was learning for the first time. She said she's gotten to know a number of people around Mohegan, including in-arena host Game Day Connor and mascot Blaze.

"[My husband and I] are huge sports fans; we love coming to the games," Elias said. "I've gotten to meet so many wonderful people. The fans are incredible, and I love coming and just seeing the women do well."

A sold-out crowd cheers during Sun's final game in Connecticut, a 95-81 win over the Toronto Tempo, on September 24, 2026 at Mohegan Sun Arena in Uncasville, Conn.Katie Morrison-O'Day

Edwards, who starred for UConn and played the last two seasons for the Sun, has been an integral part of the team's sunset season and couldn't hide her emotions after the game.

"This fan base means so much to me," Edwards said. "The support and the love have run deep since I was a freshman at UConn. It's mad love. To the fans, we want to thank you guys, because of your energy and support, even going through such a tough season...ultimately we're holding our heads up high because we're part of this legacy. Everyone today and before today made history and poured into a franchise when no one else would."

The Sun welcomed back a couple of old friends on Thursday. Former Sun forward Aneesah Morrow , who was traded to the Tempo in July, was on the bench for Toronto (she's out for the remainder of the season with a knee injury) and got a big hand from the crowd. Nykesha Sales, who played for the Sun from 2003-2007, was welcomed back and received a Sun Legends jacket before the game.

Former Sun player Nykesha Sales was honored with a Sun Legends jacket before the Connecticut Sun's final game at Mohegan Sun Arena in Uncasville, Conn. on September 24, 2026.Katie Morrison-O'Day

"The history of this franchise is not only about one team, about one coach, about one season," Sun head coach Rachid Meziane said. "[The players] know that they are part of something. I hope that people will never forget this franchise. And that's a mindset for my players tonight. Never forget what they accomplished for this franchise. Never forget the name on the front of the jersey."

Brittney Griner talks to the Sun after the team's final game in Connecticut, a 95-81 win over the Toronto Tempo, on September 24, 2026 at Mohegan Sun Arena in Uncasville, Conn.Katie Morrison-O'Day

The Sun fanbase's passion for WNBA basketball won't be confined to Mohegan Sun Arena.

"It's really emotional, but I've been saving up a lot of money for Houston, so this is definitely not my last game," Moreau said.

Elias also mentioned planning a trip to Texas to see the new team. Wilkinson talked about getting a group together for a UConn women's basketball game.

Even though the Sun has set for the final time in Connecticut, the light of the community built around the team refuses to dim.

articles.title: You are the new Scotland boss - what would you do?
articles.summary: Put yourself in the shoes of the new Scotland head coach Sebastien Pocognoli as he picks his first XI.
articles.body:
It is a new era for the Scotland men's side as head coach Sebastien Pocognoli takes charge of his first game on Saturday against Slovenia, live on the BBC.

The Belgian included eight uncapped players in his first squad before releasing Findlay Curtis and James Wilson to the under-21s, which means the line-up and approach to the Nations League match in Ljubljana is unpredictable.

However, you can try your best to assess what the new Scotland boss might do with our team selector below, while we have also picked out some key issues for Pocognoli to wrestle with.

When manager of Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco , Pocognoli generally favoured a 3-4-2-1 formation and its variations.

That means Scotland are likely to line up with three centre-backs on Saturday afternoon, with five named in the squad.

Jack Hendry and Scott McKenna are the experienced survivors from Steve Clarke's World Cup group and, given Pocognoli said he is keen to strike a balance between new and old faces "to keep the cohesion in the team", they both appear likely starters.

Especially given they have the physical profile to play the aggressive style the head coach wants.

That would leave Swansea City's Stephen Welsh , Stoke City's Luke Graham and Brondby captain Luis Binks to fight it out for the final spot.

Welsh is the only right-footed one of the three, which might give him the edge if McKenna were to play on the left and Hendry in the middle.

However, Graham has been playing on the left of a back three for Stoke, which could allow McKenna to sit in the middle and shift Hendry to the right.

It all depends what balance Scotland are looking for.

With captain Andy Robertson a certainty to win his 98th cap at left wing-back, and Aaron Hickey surely in prime position to start on the other side, where does that leave Scotland's wide attacking options?

Ben Gannon-Doak was so key for Scotland under Clarke due to his speed and ability to beat players. Josh McPake has shown a similar ability for Hearts on the same side.

However, with Pocognoli often deploying two narrow attackers either side of a centre forward and using the wing-backs for width, could Scotland's wingers be squeezed out?

One of those forward places would surely be reserved for John McGinn , given his goal threat for Scotland, running power and experience of occupying a similar role on the left. He also offers more off the ball.

Ryan Christie might be another candidate for one of those roles, assuming Scotland only play two holding midfielders from their deep pool - Lewis Ferguson and Billy Gilmour . The Bournemouth midfielder is also relentless out of possession.

Could Gannon-Doak or McPake play further in the pitch closer to a striker? And do they have the defensive instincts to play more centrally when Scotland don't have the ball?

Gannon-Doak was named as a forward in the squad, while McPake, interestingly, was named as a midfielder. Who knows if that means anything, but it will be fascinating to see what Pocognoli thinks.

Kieron Bowie , Robbie Ure and Oli McBurnie are the striker options in the squad and all three are in good form and confident.

Ure and McBurnie are yet to score for their clubs this term, but the former just got a morale-boosting move to Sevilla after his exploits in Sweden and faced Barcelona only a week ago.

The latter is playing well for Hull City in the Premier League and grabbed 19 goals in their promotion charge last term.

McBurnie is the oldest and comfortably the most experienced of the options in the squad but has never impressed in his 16 previous caps.

Now, it's a clean slate and he says he has a point to prove after a few years in the international wilderness.

It would be the ultimate vote of confidence from Pocognoli if he were to start McBurnie in the face of a few Tartan Army grumbles.

articles.title: Reds Play Spoiler, Beat Braves and Deny Atlanta No. 1 NL Playoff Seed
articles.summary: Cincinnati stunned former teammate Tyler Mahle with a power surge, powered by Elly De La Cruz’s milestone blast to topple the Braves and shuffle the postseas...
articles.body:
The Cincinnati Reds played spoiler Thursday night, beating the Braves and clinching a series win while also preventing the Braves from earning the No. 1 overall seed in the NL playoffs.

They did it against a familiar face: starting pitcher Tyler Mahle , whom the Braves acquired at the trade deadline from the San Francisco Giants . He spent the first six seasons of his career with the Reds before the Minnesota Twins acquired him at the 2022 trade deadline.

Mahle has been one of the best pitchers in baseball since August, but his former team did not treat him kindly, as they hit two home runs off Mahle and allowed five earned runs on six hits. It was the most runs Mahle had allowed since joining the Braves, with the previous high being two earned runs.

Rookie outfielder Carlos Jorge led off the game with his first career home run deep into right field. Jorge has struggled in 15 games this season, hitting below .150. Thursday's home run was also his first career RBI.

Atlanta scored for the first time off two hits by Drake Baldwin and Ronald Acuna Jr. With first and third and no outs, Matt Olson flied out to right field to score Baldwin. Michael Harris II then lined one in the left-center field gap to score Acuña Jr.

Ozzie Albies bounced to first base and saw a big blunder by the Reds, as miscommunication between Sal Stewart and starter Brady Singer led to a first and third, one-out situation. Austin Riley then drove in a run on a sacrifice fly, giving the Braves a 4-1 lead after the first inning.

Matt McLain drove in a run on a single in the second inning, cutting the Braves' lead to two.

In the third inning, just one home run and one stolen base away from his first 30/30 season, Elly De La Cruz was served up a hanging splitter on a platter and hit a ball deep into right field traveling an estimated 402 feet.

With runners on 2nd and 3rd with two outs, Eugenio Suarez stepped to the plate and lined a single into left-center field. Both Tyler Stephenson and Sal Stewart scored to give the Reds a 5-4 lead in the third inning.

Austin Riley homered off Singer in the third inning to tie the game at five. Zach McCambley came in relief of Singer and allowed a single from Mike Yastrzemski , giving the Braves the lead again, 6-5.

Reds outfielder Hector Rodriguez, who is no stranger to long home runs when he gets ahold of one, gave the Reds a 7-6 lead with a bomb to right field. AJ Smith-Shawver threw a backdoor off-speed pitch down and away to Rodriguez, who got under it and golfed it over the chop house in right field for a 423-foot shot.

Connor Phillips , Tejay Antone , Brock Burke , and Emilio Pagan combined to shut out the Braves in the final four innings, sealing the victory and clinching the series win for Cincinnati.

articles.title: Guardians’ Joey Cantillo Change Working Wonders
articles.summary: Joey Cantillo hit a rough patch in the middle of the season. But these are the Cleveland Guardians. They know how to figure pitchers out. And they have figur...
articles.body:
Joey Cantillo hit a rough patch in the middle of the season.

But these are the Cleveland Guardians . They know how to figure pitchers out. And they have figured out Cantillo.

Lately, the lefty has been much better, including in the win over the Boston Red Sox at Fenway Park on Thursday night to clinch a playoff berth for the Guardians.

If Cantillo keeps this up, he can be an asset in the postseason, even as a guy who wasn't originally making a strong enough case for such a consideration.

The Guardians decided that instead of Cantillo starting games, he should follow an opener.

It's a confusing role for many baseball fans, and it's not always clear why it works.

Yes, it usually means the longer-term pitcher comes into the game lower down in the order rather than at the top, and it also means the top hitters haven't seen Cantillo yet when he circles back to the top.

But there's also a difference in rhythm. Cantillo likely warms up at a slightly different pace. The game state feels slightly different coming in after an inning or two rather than before anything has happened yet.

For some pitchers, it's all mental, and for others, the strategic differences of following an opener really do matter.

Regardless of the reason for Cantillo, he's in the midst of delivering in a major way for the Guardians.

Thursday night is a prime example of what can work for Cantillo.

The Guardians had hard-throwing righty Daniel Espino pitch as the opener. He went 1.0 inning and struck out two, facing the minimum three hitters.

That brought up Cantillo, with the plan all along for him to follow Esipino as the bulk guy on this night.

Cantillo went 5.0 innings and allowed just 1 hit while walking 2. He struck out 4.

The Red Sox never really came close to touching him.

Cantillo threw only 47 of his 80 pitches for strikes, but he's a guy that nibbles around the zone and gets the job done in the end.

Would the Guardians go with an opener in front of Cantillo in the playoffs? If it came to that, sure. It's working wonderfully.

It might be unconventional, but the objective in the postseason is to win no matter what. No one will judge an odd choice if it works out.

Right now, the Guardians are doing everything they can to prepare for the postseason. Assessing what Cantillo can bring (and Espino as an opener) is a key point for Cleveland to have in its data set before the playoffs.

It still might not work, but at least the Guardians would consider if such a bold move would help them out, and they're giving it a shot down the stretch to feel it out for the sake of Cantillo and their entire pitching staff.

articles.title: '15 years ... I waited for long': Krishna Jaisankar set for her India moment at Asian Games
articles.summary: Whenever Krishna Jaisankar gets some time, she opens her kit bag and looks at the badge on her T-shirt. It has one word written on it: INDIA.
articles.body: Whenever Krishna Jaisankar gets some time, she opens her kit bag and looks at the badge on her T-shirt.It has one word written on it: INDIA.Every time she looks at it, her eyes get moist. But there is also a sense of confidence that builds within her. After waiting for 15 years, Krishna knows that when she finally wears the India jersey in Japan, it will mean much more than simply making her Asian Games debut.For the 23-year-old shot putter, the jersey will represent 15 years of ups and downs, missed opportunities, injuries and countless moments when she had to pick herself up and start again.“It's a surreal feeling. I just can't wait to don that jersey in Japan. 15 years.... I waited for long and yes, I have earned it. I am very appreciative, like I'm very grateful for the opportunity and to be able to finally put Team India on my back,” Krishna told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview.After missing out on selection several times, Krishna finally broke through and earned her place in the Indian team for the Asian Games 2026.Now, as she prepares to travel to Japan, the Indian shot putter wants to leave the old disappointments behind and write a new chapter - one that she hopes will end with a medal.Her message to herself when she reaches Japan is simple.“All right, it's showtime,” Krishna said.A long road to the India jerseyKrishna's journey has never been an easy one. There were moments when she wanted to give up. She left India at a young age, first moving to Jamaica and later to the United States, as she looked for opportunities to develop as an athlete.Then came the Commonwealth Games opportunity. Krishna was among the favourites to make it to the big event, but a hamstring injury disrupted her plans.She tore her hamstring just three weeks before the event. Yet, she returned to competition and managed to qualify for the Asian Games. She also became the national champion after 15 years.“I just think the fighter mentality that I have. Never to give up. Never to settle. Setbacks are meant for something. Setbacks are supposed to mould you, but not define you,” she said.Paris 2024 became a turning pointThe biggest setback came in 2024. Marred by injuries, Krishna missed the Paris Olympics. But the difficult phase also forced her to look closely at herself and rethink the way she was approaching her career.She began paying more attention to her nutrition, sleep and recovery. She also started spending more time reflecting and talking to herself.“It was a very rough period for me,” she said.“I left my country, left my family, left my comfort zone. What does my opportunity cost? What am I getting back? I'm not making the team, I'm not competing. Why am I getting injured?” she said.That period eventually changed her approach towards her ultimate goal - representing India.Instead of looking too far ahead, Krishna decided to take things one step at a time.“If you've got a dream, you've got to protect it. You have a dream, you've got to protect it,” Krishna said.From a basketball family to shot putKrishna grew up in a sporting family. Her parents, Prasanna and Jay Shankar, have been involved in basketball, and she closely watched the work they put into developing the sport. Her mother has also been a national selector for Indian basketball.But Krishna eventually chose athletics and found her own identity in shot put.“I think my inspiration was within my corners, which is my family. Whatever I am today it is because of their support. I wanted to choose a different sport and I did and I am really happy about it,” she said.“Thanks to the Reliance Foundation, the Athletics Federation of India, the Sports Development Authority of Tamil Nadu, and everyone in Tamil Nadu. Everybody has supported me and believed in me,” the 23-year-old said.Chasing Asian Games gloryMaking her Team India debut at the Asian Games is a special moment for Krishna. But she does not want the excitement of finally making the team to overshadow her bigger target - winning a medal.Once she is in Japan, she wants to treat the competition like any other championship.“Now it's go time, there is no look back. I am looking forward, looking ahead in the future,” she said.“It's going to be a show, man. It's going to be a show from all sectors of athletics. Let it be track, let it be field, we're going to put up a show. All we ask in return, support us. Keep us in your prayers,” Krishan said.Olympics - the ultimate dreamFor Krishna, the Asian Games is not the end goal. It is a start. Her bigger dream is the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.She carries an Olympic chain with her even though she is yet to compete at the Games. For her, it is a reminder of where she wants to go.“I'm not an Olympian, but every single day I aspire to be one. I'm confident now I can say that that dream is no longer a dream. It's like, I'm converting it to be a reality,” she said.The chase for 18 metresKrishna won a gold medal at the National Federation Cup 2026 and, in the process, broke her own record of 17.09m. She won the top prize with a personal best throw of 17.35m.Now, Krishna has set herself the target of crossing 18 metres. She believes the Asian Games 2026 will be a great platform to achieve that feat while also challenging for the gold medal.“I am getting closer,” she said. “But again, it's very important to believe in the process. No better place to do it than Japan. Let's have a PB in Japan. I know I am a medal contender,” she said. “So, the mindset also is walking into the thing and be like, you know what, I'm walking in as a medal contender, not as a participant,” she said.Bodyshaming: Turning comments into strengthKrishna has been muscular since childhood. Her appearance sometimes made her uncomfortable. She felt that she did not fit what she believed was society's traditional idea of how a woman should look.“I didn't even know the meaning of body shaming until, you know, somebody came and told me, hey, somebody's body shaming you,” she said.But over the years, Krishna learned to see her body differently. The same body that some people made fun of became the body that helped her break records and earn her place in Team India.“To show the world, to show the society, that the body that you're making fun of and making me feel that I'm ashamed of is the body that's helping me break records, is the body that's helping me debut for Team India at the Asian Games,” she said.Her message to young girls is direct.“Be confident in who you are. Do not change yourself for somebody. She also has another message: do not live for other people's approval. Do not seek validation from people because again, comparison is a thief of joy,” she said.'Dreams do come true'With 15 years of pain now behind her, Krishna is ready to write a new chapter in Japan. When she steps into the throwing circle with the shot in her hand, the 23-year-old will perhaps remember the 18-year-old version of herself who first dared to dream of representing India.Asked what she would say to the 18-year-old Krishna, the 23-year-old replied: “Dreams do come true”.“Know that your story is not just your journey. It's a story of so many untold stories. There are so many people that look up to you. If you have a dream, you bloody protect it,” Krishna signed off.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Klopp points to Bayern star’s costly mistake after late Netherlands equaliser
articles.summary: Serge Gnabry’s decision in the closing stages of Germany’s 1-1 draw with the Netherlands proved costly on Thursday, as the Bayern Munich attacker lost posses...
articles.body:
Serge Gnabry 's decision in the closing stages of Germany's 1-1 draw with the Netherlands proved costly on Thursday, as the Bayern Munich attacker lost possession before the Dutch side launched the counter-attack that led to their late equaliser.

Speaking in a post-match interview, Germany coach Jürgen Klopp suggested that Gnabry knows he should have handled the situation differently.

"That's not a problem, it can happen. But Serge has to run forward in that moment," Klopp explained.

"He has to take his first touch forward with the ball when you still have 20 or 30 seconds to play. But Serge obviously knows that too."

Lothar Matthäus also highlighted Gnabry's role in the Dutch equaliser.

"That was a great attack, but Gnabry must not lose the ball and he has to track back faster," the former Germany international said in his role as an RTL pundit.

articles.title: “He didn’t get that from his dad” – Klopp takes cheeky dig at Bayern legend after Ruben van Bommel’s brilliant assist
articles.summary: Ruben van Bommel played a key role in the Netherlands’ 1-1 equaliser against Germany on Thursday, with the 22-year-old midfielder’s clever pass setting up Co...
articles.body:
Ruben van Bommel played a key role in the Netherlands' 1-1 equaliser against Germany on Thursday, with the 22-year-old midfielder's clever pass setting up Cody Gakpo to level the score.

The PSV midfielder subsequently drew praise from Germany coach Jürgen Klopp, who also used the occasion to take a playful dig at the player's father, Mark van Bommel, who played for Bayern Munich between 2006 and 2011.

"Sensational pass from van Bommel. He didn't get that from his dad. The outside-of-the-foot technique must come from his mother," Klopp said with a grin.

Klopp was alluding to the fact that Mark van Bommel, a 79-time Netherlands international , made his name with very different qualities. Tough tackling and aggression were more his trademark than delicate technique and pinpoint passing.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: India assured themselves of three squash medals at the Asian Games 2026 on Friday as Joshna Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar entered the mixed doubles semifinals, while Anahat Singh and Abhay Singh advanced to the last four in the women’s and men’s singles respectively.For Joshna, the semifinal berth carried added significance. The 40-year-old, competing at her record seventh Asian Games, secured her sixth medal at the continental showpiece with Senthilkumar. The Indian duo produced a dominant 11-3, 11-5 win over the Philippines’ David Pelino and Jemyca Aribado in their quarterfinal.Junior world champion Anahat and Abhay also continued their campaigns with straight-game victories, leaving India with three medal assurances across the squash events.Asian Games Full Coverage | Medal Tally | ScheduleJoshna seals sixth Asian Games medalJoshna and Senthilkumar needed less than half an hour to dispatch the Philippine pair at the Nagoya Kinjo Futo Arena. The Indians took control from the start, racing to a 3-0 lead and quickly extending it to 9-2 before wrapping up the opening game 11-3 in nine minutes.The second game was more competitive initially, with Pelino and Aribado reducing the deficit to 4-2. But Joshna and Senthilkumar shifted gears again, moving to 7-2 and then 8-4 before closing out the match 11-5.They will face Hong Kong’s Yo Ka Lee and Ming Hong Tang in Saturday’s semifinal.“Winning a medal for your country is always very special. And that's been my motivation all my career,” Joshna told PTI after the match.The medal will take Joshna’s Asian Games tally to six, including two silver. Her previous medals include a singles bronze in 2018, team silver in 2014 and 2018, and team bronze in 2010 and 2022.Joshna has now surpassed Saurav Ghosal’s record of six Asian Games appearances, having competed at every edition since the 2002 Busan Games.Anahat, Abhay march into singles semifinalsAnahat continued her impressive campaign with a commanding 11-2, 11-5, 11-3 victory over compatriot Tanvi Khanna in the women’s singles quarterfinal.The junior world champion and medal favourite will now look to take another step towards the gold medal and a potential Olympic qualification. The singles gold medallists at the Asian Games will directly qualify for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, where squash will make its Olympic debut.In the men’s singles, Abhay overcame local favourite Ryonosuke Tsukue 11-4, 11-3, 11-6 to book his place in the last four.He will face Pakistan’s Irfan Muhammad, who defeated India’s Veer Chotrani 6-11, 11-8, 11-3, 11-3 in 41 minutes after recovering from a game down.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: How Carsley aims to lead England to U21 glory - for third time in row
articles.summary: Lee Carsley is aware of the challenge ahead, but also the lasting impact more success with England Under-21s could have.
articles.body:
Lee Carsley has yet to get his picture on the wall at St George's Park.

At England 's base, there are framed photographs of every senior England manager, which line opposite sides of a corridor. All of them - from Walter Winterbottom to Sam Allardyce, who was in charge for only one game - are included.

Despite winning back-to-back European Championships with England Under-21s, however, the Young Lions boss is still absent. He even managed the senior side for six games after Gareth Southgate's departure.

Yet Carsley is not concerned with personal accolades as he plots a treble with the under-21s.

Victories against Kazakhstan, at Wolves ' Molineux Stadium on Friday, and Slovakia next week will book a spot at Euro 2027 - and keep Carsley and his players on course for history.

Embracing the expectation of two-time champions

England lifted successive trophies in 1982 and 1984 but then had to wait 39 years until Carsley's men won in Georgia and Romania in 2023, beating Spain in the final.

Last summer's extra-time victory over Germany in Bratislava sealed their title defence, thanks to Jonathan Rowe 's strike.

Winning the tournament three times in a row has only ever been done once before, by Italy in the 1990s, although never in the competition's current guise of 16 teams.

Carsley is aware of the challenge ahead - but also the lasting impact more success could have.

"The older you get, you want to leave a legacy, don't you?" He said, with England top of Group D and three points clear of Slovakia.

"There would have been an easy move, after the first win, to go and do club management and go and accept a few of the offers.

"But I enjoy the job I'm doing and I enjoy that I'm part of a bigger quest to win a major tournament. I want to be part of the FA when we do that."

Carsley also says he welcomes the pressure of attempting to do something no Young Lions team has done before.

"I think we have to embrace that," said the former Everton and Derby midfielder. "They come to play for the under-21s, you're back-to-back champions. There's a bullseye that goes with that. We have to be aware of that and go for it.

"The expectancy, we'll just get through the group and then we'll win the quarters, we'll win the semis and then we'll just win the final... it's very difficult.

"My priority is definitely qualifying and then that's something I'll think about."

England started their qualifying campaign with a 2-0 win in Kazakhstan last September, although they have not played since beating Moldova in March.

The Young Lions host Slovakia in Stoke on 2 October before travelling to Cork to wrap up Group D against Ireland four days later.

They have won six of their seven games, but needed an injury-time Rico Lewis penalty to rescue a 1-1 draw in Andorra in March.

Like Lewis, there are plenty of recognisable names within the current squad, including Tottenham's Archie Gray and Dortmund 's Jobe Bellingham .

It is noteworthy how many of the recent England Under-21 winners have gone on to represent the senior side - particularly the 2023 squad, which featured Cole Palmer and Anthony Gordon .

Noni Madueke , who featured in this year's World Cup, could not even get in the starting XI.

But their triumphs in 2023 and 2025 were not without nervy moments.

They only won Group F by a point in Euro 2025 qualifying, needing two late goals by James McAtee to beat Ukraine in their penultimate game to take the race for top spot to the final match.

They then beat Azerbaijan 7-0, as Ukraine lost 1-0 to Serbia, to overhaul their rivals and top the group.

Carsley is refusing to take anything for granted this time.

"We can't just be arrogant and think, we'll just turn up, we've got better players," he said.

"We've got to make sure we constantly make these players aware we are a big scalp, this is a chance for them to make a big deal in their own country, so it's important mentally and physically you're ready to challenge.

"It's very difficult to qualify. I've never known an easy qualification process, but sometimes you forget - when you're on the pitch and you've got the trophy in your hands - the journey you've gone on to get there."
